thread.title_full: Illusions Don't Keep the Peace - Commentary Magazine

author: Brian Stewart
title: Illusions Don't Keep the Peace - Commentary Magazine
text:
At various points in the 20th century, liberal writers and politicians blithely predicted the end of war. The British journalist Norman Angell argued that the interconnected economies of Europe would prevent the outbreak of war or at least curtail its duration when organized social and economic life ground to a halt because of it. He said this in 1910; four years later came the most wide-ranging and deadly war the world had ever seen. In 1928, the Kellogg-Briand Pact went so far as to “outlaw” war. Sixty-two nations signed it. Eight years later, the Nazis began to move on their neighbors. There was a similar frenzy of optimism in the West after World War II, as the United Nations came into being while advocates of a one-world government argued that a pacific planet was a genuine possibility.
Eliot Cohen is too wise a student of history and human nature to indulge such fantastic and utopian notions. He has spent many years educating students about the violent and well-nigh eternal competition for power in the international system. He has also brought his trademark realism to bear as a policy practitioner, having served in the intelligence community and the Department of Defense. His new book, The Strategist, is a subtle and studious guide about “how to think about war and politics” in our own time.
Cohen begins by casting a jaundiced eye on trendy theories about delivering mankind from the menace of war, especially after the collapse of the Soviet Union. This epochal moment led otherwise clever people to imagine an escape from the burdens of power and the tragic realities of human existence. Intellectuals warned that war had become ineffective in our globalized world. Fareed Zakaria spoke for many when he argued (on the eve of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Islamic State’s creation of a caliphate across Syria and Iraq) that “there is an evolving international order with new global norms making war and conquest increasingly rare.”
“Experience,” Cohen observes in The Strategist, “delivered painful rebuttals to these hopes.” The violent and savage struggles of our time suggest that the desire to avoid war, which has justified policies of appeasement toward hostile foreign powers and a crabbed view of the national interest and, has not helped keep the peace. On the contrary, by demonstrating weakness and provoking the world’s revisionist regimes, the lingering passivity of U.S. foreign policy after the Cold War has set the stage for a new era of great-power conflict. The Strategist aims to stir a rebirth of strategic thinking that may yet prevent the premature eclipse of Pax Americana.
In an era of widespread ignorance of and dismissiveness toward the subject of warfare, this emphasis on the utility of force, or the threat of force, is refreshing. Cohen’s call for “a new look at the problem of strategic thought and action” is especially timely because the concept of “strategy” has been promiscuously abused of late, and the word itself, as he sagely warns, “is in danger of losing its meaning.”
Rather than accepting that organized violence is a permanent feature of mankind, Cohen argues that the West has embraced a Kantian vision of permanent peace. During the protracted post–Cold War “holiday” from history, the preparation and the real or threatened use of armed force to serve political ends have withered. Cohen laments that the modern aversion to conflict has led logically and naturally to a pervasive sense of futility about war that “has had a real and deleterious effect on our ability to think straight about strategy.” Just as Clausewitz taught that “war cannot be divorced from political life,” so the rejection of war is ultimately a rejection of politics.
In The Strategist, Cohen seeks to restore a sense of balance and spirit in the American worldview, in part by educating citizens about the inherent trade-offs between power and values in a fallen world. At a time when a majority of Americans believe peace is the natural condition of the world, and that the liberal order will continue bereft of robust U.S. global leadership, the beginning of wisdom is to recognize that the tension between force and morality in international politics is inescapable, and that justice without power is doomed. Politics is the area, as Reinhold Niebuhr wrote, where conscience and power will always meet, “where the ethical and coercive factors of human life will interpenetrate and work out their tentative and uneasy compromises.”
This complex fate of wielding power in our own defense and on behalf of a modicum of freedom in the international commons should not be too tall an order for Americans. Since the dawn of the republic, leading American statesmen have fused the concepts of power and justice, embracing the notion of an “empire of liberty.” Theodore Roosevelt insisted on “combining power with high purpose” as he oversaw the expansion of American military might. The postwar architects of the U.S. policy of containment, chastened by the collapse of world order during the interwar era, believed that only tragic vigilance could protect the free world while aggressive totalitarian forces reigned across more than half of the Eurasian continent.
Many modern readers, steeped in a therapeutic reading of history and human affairs, will resist the need for strategic thinking and the realism that underlies it. But it’s hardly outlandish to believe, as Cohen does, that “human beings and states seem to be hardwired for war.” Will and Ariel Durant reluctantly drew the same conclusion when in 1968 they calculated that there had been only 268 years free of war in the previous 3,421. Any thinking person will find it hard to quarrel with Cohen’s somber view that “the unfortunate fact is that war is with us and will remain so for the foreseeable future.”
And if war is fated to be with us, then it behooves democratic publics to relearn the ways of strategy, to pluck down their dusty copies of Clausewitz from the bookshelves, and to harness military means in the defense of our interests and values. The alternative to rediscovering strategic thought and action at this historical juncture will not be pleasant. At present, cruel and rapacious tyrannical regimes the world over are mastering the dark art of power and preparing to deploy vast resources to the detriment of our way of life.
For sounding the alarm about that grave impending danger, and for throwing a floodlight on how a formidable strategy can protect a fragile world order, Eliot Cohen has done us an extraordinary service with The Strategist.
